title: Local Coverage Governs Memorization in Diffusion Models
abstract: Memorization in diffusion models is often treated as a global property of the model or dataset. In practice, however, a single diffusion model can simultaneously generate both memorized and novel samples. Which training samples are most likely to be memorized? In this work, we show that memorization is governed by \emph{local data coverage}. Leveraging the connection between diffusion models and kernel density estimation (KDE), we derive a theoretical criterion that predicts whether a point is memorized based on the density of training data in its neighborhood and the size of the training dataset. In the high-dimensional limit, this leads to a sharp, local transition: regions of low coverage are dominated by isolated training samples, which are memorized, while dense regions support interpolation and generalization. We validate these predictions empirically, showing that memorization increases with local sparsity and that diffusion models exhibit a coexistence of memorized and novel samples within the same model. Extending this framework to multi-class settings, we further show that classes with higher intra-class sparsity (and thus lower local coverage) are more strongly memorized. Our results provide a local view of memorization in diffusion models, explaining when and where memorization occurs in terms of data geometry.
summary: This paper develops a local theory demonstrating that memorization in diffusion models is dictated by the local data coverage—specifically, regions with low data density are more likely to memorize training samples. By connecting the model's behavior to Kernel Density Estimation, it provides a quantitative framework explaining the coexistence of generalization and rote memorization within a single generative process.
main_problem: The work aims to move beyond treating memorization in diffusion models as a global property, instead establishing that it is governed by the local data coverage of the training manifold.
main_result: Memorization occurs preferentially in regions of low local data coverage (high sparsity), while dense regions support generalization and interpolation. This relationship can be theoretically derived using connections to Kernel Density Estimation (KDE).
method: The authors combine theoretical derivations based on the exponential transform of KDE with empirical validation using metrics like local dominance and nearest-neighbor statistics.
model_or_system: The system is a Diffusion Model trained on finite image datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, CelebA). The analysis treats the model's learned density estimation process as analogous to Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) operating in high dimensions.
key_observables: Local data coverage ($ho_{in}(x)$), local sparsity, local dominance ($\Delta$), and the memorization rate (based on nearest-neighbor distances).
important_parameters: The ratio of local density to sample complexity parameter ($\alpha$); the threshold $	au$ used for defining memorization based on distance ratios.
main_assumptions: The theoretical analysis relies on high-dimensional limits ($N 	o \infty$) and specific scaling assumptions regarding the relationship between data points and the KDE approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that local dominance increases with sparsity, confirming that sparse regions are prone to single-sample retrieval (memorization), while dense regions show interpolation behavior. Multi-class settings show class diversity correlating with memorization risk.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the global limitation of prior work to developing a local theory linking memorization to KDE statistics, providing mathematical proofs for the transition regimes, and finally validating these predictions across multiple image datasets using geometric metrics.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, geometry-based understanding of model failure modes (memorization) in deep generative models by mapping them onto established concepts from statistical physics like local density estimation and phase transitions.
